records.title: Free fall in a uniform gravitational field
records.subject: Physics
records.shortDescription: Free fall is motion under gravity alone. In a near-Earth uniform field, a body released from rest accelerates downward at g.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Imagine letting go of a ball where air has no effect. It falls faster each second because Earth pulls it downward.
explanation: Free fall is motion under gravity alone. In a near-Earth uniform field, a body released from rest accelerates downward at g.
Taking downward as positive, v=gt and distance fallen=½gt², until ground contact. The model uses g=9.81 m/s²; it excludes air resistance and variation in gravity.
In an evacuated drop tube, objects of different masses released together have equal acceleration.
scientificPrinciples: Taking downward as positive, v=gt and distance fallen=½gt², until ground contact. The model uses g=9.81 m/s²; it excludes air resistance and variation in gravity.

definitions.Uniform field: A region where gravitational acceleration has the same magnitude and direction.

records.formula: v = gt; s = ½gt²; v² = 2gs · v m/s, s m, t s
realLifeExamples: In an evacuated drop tube, objects of different masses released together have equal acceleration.
objectives: Start at rest at the selected height.
Equal time intervals cover increasing distances.
Keep height fixed and compare two masses.
prerequisites: SI units and careful observation
misconceptions: A heavier object does not have greater free-fall acceleration in this uniform-field model.

records.title: Air resistance
records.subject: Physics
records.shortDescription: Air resistance opposes a body’s velocity relative to air. For this falling-body model, drag increases with the square of speed.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Air pushes against a falling object. A wider object feels more resistance at the same speed.
explanation: Air resistance opposes a body’s velocity relative to air. For this falling-body model, drag increases with the square of speed.
For downward speed v, Fdrag=½ρCdAv² upward and acceleration=g−Fdrag/m. Air density and drag coefficient are fixed teaching assumptions.
A broad parachute slows descent by increasing frontal area; this model does not calculate deployment.
scientificPrinciples: For downward speed v, Fdrag=½ρCdAv² upward and acceleration=g−Fdrag/m. Air density and drag coefficient are fixed teaching assumptions.

definitions.Drag: Force resisting relative motion through a fluid.
definitions.Frontal area: Projected area facing the flow, measured in m².

records.formula: Fdrag = ½ρCdAv²; a = g − Fdrag/m
realLifeExamples: A broad parachute slows descent by increasing frontal area; this model does not calculate deployment.
objectives: At zero speed, quadratic drag is zero.
Compare drag with weight.
A finite drop may end before terminal speed.
prerequisites: SI units and careful observation
misconceptions: Air resistance is not constant, and it does not point upward for every possible direction of motion.

records.title: Terminal velocity
records.subject: Physics
records.shortDescription: Terminal velocity occurs when drag balances weight, so vertical acceleration becomes zero while the body continues moving.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: A falling object can reach a steady speed when the air’s upward push balances its weight.
explanation: Terminal velocity occurs when drag balances weight, so vertical acceleration becomes zero while the body continues moving.
For a body falling in still air with quadratic drag and negligible buoyancy, vt=√(2mg/(ρCdA)). The solution approaches vt; a short tower may be insufficient.
Skydivers change posture to change area and hence terminal speed; the model represents a fixed posture.
scientificPrinciples: For a body falling in still air with quadratic drag and negligible buoyancy, vt=√(2mg/(ρCdA)). The solution approaches vt; a short tower may be insufficient.

definitions.Terminal speed: Steady limiting speed when the net force is zero.

records.formula: vt = √(2mg / ρCdA) · m/s
realLifeExamples: Skydivers change posture to change area and hence terminal speed; the model represents a fixed posture.
objectives: Weight acts downward throughout descent.
At the limit, drag equals weight.
Compare mass and area separately.
prerequisites: SI units and careful observation
misconceptions: Zero acceleration does not mean zero velocity.

records.title: Buoyancy
records.subject: Physics
records.shortDescription: Buoyancy is the resultant upward pressure force exerted by a fluid on an immersed object.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Water pushes harder on the bottom of a submerged object than on its top, creating an upward force.
explanation: Buoyancy is the resultant upward pressure force exerted by a fluid on an immersed object.
In a stationary uniform-density fluid, Fb=ρfluid g Vdisplaced. A freely floating object balances weight with buoyancy; a held object may need another force.
A floating boat displaces enough water for the displaced water’s weight to equal the boat’s weight.
scientificPrinciples: In a stationary uniform-density fluid, Fb=ρfluid g Vdisplaced. A freely floating object balances weight with buoyancy; a held object may need another force.

definitions.Buoyancy: Net upward hydrostatic force on an immersed object.
definitions.Displaced volume: Volume of fluid excluded by the submerged part.

records.formula: Fb = ρfluid g Vdisplaced · N
realLifeExamples: A floating boat displaces enough water for the displaced water’s weight to equal the boat’s weight.
objectives: Identify the submerged part.
Multiply fluid density, g and displaced volume.
At fixed volume, denser fluid produces more buoyancy.
prerequisites: SI units and careful observation
misconceptions: Buoyancy depends on displaced volume and fluid density, not on object mass alone.

records.title: Archimedes principle
records.subject: Physics
records.shortDescription: Archimedes’ principle states that buoyant force equals the weight of the fluid displaced by an immersed body.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Imagine replacing the underwater part of an object with water. That water’s weight tells you the upward buoyant force.
explanation: Archimedes’ principle states that buoyant force equals the weight of the fluid displaced by an immersed body.
The principle follows from hydrostatic pressure forces. Displaced-fluid mass is ρV, and its weight is ρgV; partial and complete immersion use the same rule.
A ship’s hull can contain air while its total mass is supported by the water displaced by the submerged hull.
scientificPrinciples: The principle follows from hydrostatic pressure forces. Displaced-fluid mass is ρV, and its weight is ρgV; partial and complete immersion use the same rule.
records.formula: Fb = mdisplaced g = ρVdisplaced g
realLifeExamples: A ship’s hull can contain air while its total mass is supported by the water displaced by the submerged hull.
objectives: Read its density in kg/m³.
Multiply density by displaced volume.
Double immersion before full submergence.
prerequisites: SI units and careful observation
misconceptions: The displaced-fluid volume equals submerged object volume, not necessarily the entire object volume.

steps.title: Define the fluid
steps.caption: Read its density in kg/m³.
steps.detail: Density and volume must use compatible units.

steps.title: Find displacement
steps.caption: Use only the submerged volume.
steps.detail: A partially immersed block displaces less than its full volume.

steps.title: Find fluid mass
steps.caption: Multiply density by displaced volume.
steps.detail: The result has units of kilograms.

steps.title: Find fluid weight
steps.caption: Multiply displaced mass by g.
steps.detail: This equals the buoyant force.

steps.title: Test proportionality
steps.caption: Double immersion before full submergence.
steps.detail: Buoyancy doubles in the uniform liquid.

records.title: Apparent loss in weight
records.subject: Physics
records.shortDescription: A suspended object has a smaller support-force reading in a fluid because buoyancy provides part of the upward force.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: A hanging scale pulls upward less strongly when water also supports the object.
explanation: A suspended object has a smaller support-force reading in a fluid because buoyancy provides part of the upward force.
At rest with upward support, T=mg−Fb. The apparent loss in weight is W−T=Fb. Negative support means a downward restraint is needed; an ordinary string cannot push down.
A dense stone suspended from a spring balance reads less when submerged.
scientificPrinciples: At rest with upward support, T=mg−Fb. The apparent loss in weight is W−T=Fb. Negative support means a downward restraint is needed; an ordinary string cannot push down.

definitions.Apparent weight: Support-force reading, not a change in gravitational mass.
definitions.Tension: Pulling force exerted by a taut string.

records.formula: T = mg − ρgVdisplaced; W − T = Fb
realLifeExamples: A dense stone suspended from a spring balance reads less when submerged.
objectives: Find W=mg.

misconceptions: Immersion does not reduce the object’s mass or its gravitational weight in the model.

records.title: Angle of contact
records.subject: Physics
records.shortDescription: Contact angle describes how a liquid surface meets a solid, measured through the liquid. It helps determine whether a narrow tube shows capillary rise or depression.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: A liquid can curve upward or downward where it touches a wall. The angle at that meeting point matters.
explanation: Contact angle describes how a liquid surface meets a solid, measured through the liquid. It helps determine whether a narrow tube shows capillary rise or depression.
In an ideal cylindrical tube, h=2γcosθ/(ρgr). Angles below 90° give rise, above 90° give depression, and 90° gives no net capillary height in this model.
Clean water on glass commonly wets the wall; actual angles depend on surface chemistry and contamination.
scientificPrinciples: In an ideal cylindrical tube, h=2γcosθ/(ρgr). Angles below 90° give rise, above 90° give depression, and 90° gives no net capillary height in this model.

definitions.Contact angle: Angle between solid surface and liquid-interface tangent, measured through the liquid.
definitions.Wetting: Tendency of a liquid to spread over or adhere to a solid.

records.formula: h = 2γ cosθ / (ρgr) · θ in degrees in the controls
realLifeExamples: Clean water on glass commonly wets the wall; actual angles depend on surface chemistry and contamination.
objectives: Identify solid, liquid and gas.
An angle below 90° gives positive height.
The equation predicts equilibrium height.
prerequisites: SI units and careful observation
misconceptions: Contact angle is measured through the liquid, and it is not always zero.

detailedExplanation: Rutherford scattering reveals that atomic positive charge and most mass are concentrated in a very small nucleus.

This model treats an alpha particle and a fixed gold nucleus as repelling point charges. The classical angle satisfies cot(θ/2)=2Eb/(kq1q2); electron screening, nuclear recoil and strong interactions are omitted.

records.title: Ionic bonding

explanation: Activation energy is the energy-scale parameter in the Arrhenius relation for a reaction pathway.

A catalysed route can have a different effective activation energy; a real multi-step mechanism may not show one constant Ea.

records.title: Chemical equilibrium
records.subject: Chemistry
records.shortDescription: Chemical equilibrium is a dynamic state in which forward and reverse reaction rates are equal and macroscopic concentrations remain constant.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Particles keep changing both ways even when the amounts stop changing overall.
explanation: Chemical equilibrium is a dynamic state in which forward and reverse reaction rates are equal and macroscopic concentrations remain constant.
For this closed reversible first-order A⇌B model, d[B]/dt=kf[A]−kr[B], [A]+[B]=Ctotal and K=[B]eq/[A]eq=kf/kr. More complicated stoichiometries require different expressions.
Reversible reactions can approach the same equilibrium from either side under fixed conditions.

records.title: Solubility
records.subject: Chemistry
records.shortDescription: Solubility describes the amount of a substance that can dissolve at specified conditions. This investigation focuses on a dilute gas dissolved in a liquid.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: A liquid can hold more of some gases when the gas above it is at higher partial pressure.
explanation: Solubility describes the amount of a substance that can dissolve at specified conditions. This investigation focuses on a dilute gas dissolved in a liquid.

For the chosen dilute, nonreacting gas at fixed temperature, Henry’s law is Ceq=kH pgas. The approach C(t)=Ceq(1−e⁻ᵏᵗ) is a chosen well-mixed transfer model. Solid solubility and reactive gases need different descriptions.
Carbonated drinks illustrate pressure-dependent dissolved gas, but CO₂ chemistry and bubbles are more complex than this ideal dilute model.
scientificPrinciples: For the chosen dilute, nonreacting gas at fixed temperature, Henry’s law is Ceq=kH pgas. The approach C(t)=Ceq(1−e⁻ᵏᵗ) is a chosen well-mixed transfer model. Solid solubility and reactive gases need different descriptions.

definitions.Solubility: Equilibrium dissolved amount under specified conditions.

records.title: Radioactivity
records.subject: Physics
records.shortDescription: Radioactive decay is a spontaneous nuclear transformation; a population has a predictable exponential expectation even though individual decay times are random.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: You cannot predict which unstable nucleus decays next, but many nuclei show a characteristic half-life.
explanation: Radioactive decay is a spontaneous nuclear transformation; a population has a predictable exponential expectation even though individual decay times are random.

The expected undecayed population is N=N0exp(−λt), with λ=ln2/t½ and activity λN. The displayed dot changes represent a deterministic expectation, not individual random predictions or a radiation-dose calculation.
Radioisotopes are used as tracers and for dating when an appropriate decay model and calibrated half-life apply.

detailedExplanation: Radioactive decay is a spontaneous nuclear transformation; a population has a predictable exponential expectation even though individual decay times are random.

records.title: Surface tension
records.subject: Physics
records.shortDescription: Separate liquid, solid wall and gas.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Surface tension describes an interface’s resistance to increasing area and the associated force per unit length.
explanation: Separate liquid, solid wall and gas.

records.title: Distance and displacement
records.subject: Physics
records.shortDescription: Fix an origin before the motion.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Distance is accumulated path length; displacement is the vector from initial to final position.
explanation: Fix an origin before the motion.

For a curved projectile path, travelled distance is longer than the magnitude of displacement between its endpoints. Average speed is total distance/time, while average velocity is displacement/time. These distinctions apply before and after a return to the launch height.
Walking around a closed track gives positive distance and zero final displacement.
scientificPrinciples: For a curved projectile path, travelled distance is longer than the magnitude of displacement between its endpoints. Average speed is total distance/time, while average velocity is displacement/time. These distinctions apply before and after a return to the launch height.

definitions.Distance: Nonnegative length of the travelled path.
definitions.Displacement: Vector difference between final and initial position.

records.formula: Δr = rfinal−rinitial; |Δr| ≤ path length
realLifeExamples: Walking around a closed track gives positive distance and zero final displacement.
objectives: Fix an origin before the motion.
Displacement ignores the intermediate route.
Use distance for average speed and displacement for average velocity.
prerequisites: SI units and careful observation
misconceptions: Returning to the starting height does not imply zero displacement if the horizontal position has changed.

records.title: Continuity equation
records.subject: Physics
records.shortDescription: Compare two cross-sections of one steady stream.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: The continuity equation expresses conservation of mass in fluid flow.
explanation: Compare two cross-sections of one steady stream.

records.shortDescription: The membrane separates two compartments.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: A cell membrane forms a selectively permeable boundary between cytoplasm and surroundings.
explanation: The membrane separates two compartments.

records.title: Planetary motion

records.shortDescription: The dominant mass sits at one focus of the ellipse.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Planetary motion under a dominant central gravitational mass follows Keplerian geometry to a useful approximation.
explanation: The dominant mass sits at one focus of the ellipse.

A bound ellipse has semimajor axis a and eccentricity e<1; a central body at a focus is swept out with constant areal velocity. For the fixed solar-mass units in this model, period in days is 365.256a^(3/2), with a in AU. Mutual perturbations are omitted.
A more eccentric orbit moves faster near perihelion and more slowly near aphelion.

The scene solves the ideal two-body Kepler problem.

records.shortDescription: How does pendulum length affect period?
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Scientific investigations use questions, testable ideas, evidence and revision. This pendulum study tests how length affects period.
explanation: How does pendulum length affect period?

For small angular displacements the ideal pendulum period is 2π√(L/g). The model excludes damping and uses a small-angle approximation; changing one variable at a time makes comparisons easier, while repeated real measurements reveal variability.
A prediction that quadrupling length doubles period can be checked against observations.

records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Simple machines help redirect forces or trade force against movement distance. A lever turns about a fulcrum.

The ideal lever compares torque from perpendicular forces at selected arm lengths. Balance requires equal opposing torques. The model does not create energy or include friction, bending or a complete work-through-displacement calculation.
A seesaw can balance unequal loads by changing their distances from the pivot.

records.title: Work energy power
records.subject: Physics
records.shortDescription: A stretched spring stores elastic energy.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Work transfers energy when a force acts through displacement. Power is the rate of energy transfer.
explanation: A stretched spring stores elastic energy.

The ideal undamped spring exchanges elastic potential energy and kinetic energy while their sum stays constant. Spring force is −kx; work done by that force equals the decrease in elastic potential energy. Instantaneous power is Fv and can have either sign.
A compressed ideal spring accelerates an attached mass as elastic energy becomes kinetic energy.
scientificPrinciples: The ideal undamped spring exchanges elastic potential energy and kinetic energy while their sum stays constant. Spring force is −kx; work done by that force equals the decrease in elastic potential energy. Instantaneous power is Fv and can have either sign.

definitions.Work: Energy transferred by a force through displacement.
definitions.Power: Rate of work or energy transfer.

records.formula: K=½mv²; U=½kx²; Wspring=−ΔU; P=Fv
realLifeExamples: A compressed ideal spring accelerates an attached mass as elastic energy becomes kinetic energy.
objectives: A stretched spring stores elastic energy.
Speed and kinetic energy are greatest.

records.shortDescription: The first finger represents magnetic field direction.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Fleming’s left-hand rule relates magnetic field, conventional current and force for a motor conductor.

records.shortDescription: Identify lens, optical axis and focal points.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Ray diagrams locate ideal optical images using selected representative rays and their intersections or backward extensions.
explanation: Identify lens, optical axis and focal points.

records.title: Total internal reflection
records.subject: Physics
records.shortDescription: Set the incident medium to higher refractive index.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Total internal reflection can occur when light travels from a higher refractive index to a lower one beyond the critical angle.
explanation: Set the incident medium to higher refractive index.

Snell’s law gives n1 sinθ1=n2 sinθ2. When n1>n2 and sinθ1>n2/n1, there is no propagating refracted ray in the second medium. This flat lossless model gives unit reflected power in TIR; it does not visualize the evanescent field.
Optical fibres can guide light using total internal reflection under suitable index and angle conditions.
scientificPrinciples: Snell’s law gives n1 sinθ1=n2 sinθ2. When n1>n2 and sinθ1>n2/n1, there is no propagating refracted ray in the second medium. This flat lossless model gives unit reflected power in TIR; it does not visualize the evanescent field.

definitions.Critical angle: Incidence angle giving a refracted angle of 90° for n1>n2.
definitions.Total internal reflection: Complete reflection of incident power in this ideal lossless interface case.

realLifeExamples: Optical fibres can guide light using total internal reflection under suitable index and angle conditions.

records.title: Electric charge

records.shortDescription: The ideal system redistributes charge.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Electric charge is a conserved property of matter. Charge transfer can leave objects with positive or negative net charge.

records.title: Alternating current
records.subject: Physics
records.shortDescription: The angular speed is prescribed.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Alternating current reverses direction periodically. A rotating-coil generator can produce a sinusoidal induced voltage.
explanation: The angular speed is prescribed.

A prescribed coil rotates uniformly in a uniform magnetic field. Flux per turn is BA cosωt, induced emf is NBAω sinωt, and a purely resistive load gives I=emf/R. Inductance, capacitance, back-reaction and mechanical-drive power are omitted.
An AC generator changes the sign of its emf each half turn.

records.title: Kinetic theory
records.subject: Physics
records.shortDescription: The gas contains many moving particles.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Kinetic theory connects macroscopic gas properties with microscopic particle motion and collisions.
explanation: The gas contains many moving particles.

For an ideal monatomic gas, mean translational kinetic energy per particle is 3kBT/2 and pV=NkBT=nRT. The viewer calculates the ideal-gas state equation; particle animation is illustrative, not a numerical collision simulation or a measured speed distribution.
At the same temperature, ideal gas species have the same mean translational kinetic energy but different typical speeds if particle masses differ.

records.title: Cells and organelles

records.shortDescription: Find its enclosing plasma membrane.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Cells are living units with a membrane, genetic information and machinery that supports life. Eukaryotic cells contain specialized compartments.

records.title: Cell division
records.subject: Biology
records.shortDescription: DNA replication occurs before mitosis.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Cell division produces new cells. In the eukaryotic mitotic cycle, replicated chromosomes are separated before cytoplasmic division.
explanation: DNA replication occurs before mitosis.

DNA replication precedes mitosis. Mitosis distributes sister copies into daughter nuclei; cytokinesis divides cytoplasm. The displayed mitotic example preserves ploidy and is distinct from meiosis and bacterial binary fission.
Growth and tissue renewal rely on regulated cell division.

records.title: Xylem and phloem

records.shortDescription: Follow the blue water pathway.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Xylem and phloem are complex vascular tissues transporting different materials between plant regions.
explanation: Follow the blue water pathway.

records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Hybridization is a localized bonding description combining atomic orbitals into directional forms. Geometry and hybridization are related models rather than visible electron paths.

Methane’s tetrahedral bonding arrangement is commonly described using sp³ hybrids.

records.shortDescription: The model soil is fully saturated.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Soil contains mineral particles, organic matter, water, air and organisms. Its structure affects storage and movement of water.
explanation: The model soil is fully saturated.

The investigation uses a fully saturated homogeneous column with prescribed hydraulic conductivity, porosity, length and total head drop. Darcy’s law gives volumetric flow, and pore speed is Darcy flux divided by porosity. It does not model unsaturated infiltration, erosion or identify a soil solely from conductivity.
Two saturated columns with different conductivity can pass water at different rates under the same head gradient.
scientificPrinciples: The investigation uses a fully saturated homogeneous column with prescribed hydraulic conductivity, porosity, length and total head drop. definitions.Hydraulic conductivity: Coefficient relating hydraulic-head gradient to Darcy water flux.

records.formula: Q=K A Δh/L; pore-water speed=(Q/A)/porosity
realLifeExamples: Two saturated columns with different conductivity can pass water at different rates under the same head gradient.

Two saturated columns with different conductivity can pass water at different rates under the same head gradient.
Darcy flux is not the same as mean pore-water speed, and saturated flow is not an unsaturated wetting-front model.

records.title: Living and nonliving

records.shortDescription: Observe more than one characteristic.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Living organisms have cellular organization and coordinated life processes. Several properties must be considered together.
explanation: Observe more than one characteristic.

Energy processing, regulation, response, growth, reproduction across lineages and evolution help characterize life. A viable dormant seed remains living despite little visible activity; an individual need not reproduce to be alive. Flames use energy and spread without being cellular organisms. Viruses are acellular and host-dependent.
A plant is living even when it shows no obvious movement.

records.subject: Biology
records.shortDescription: Locate the heart and kidneys.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Circulation supplies blood to organs, including kidneys, while excretion removes metabolic wastes and helps regulate internal conditions.
explanation: Locate the heart and kidneys.

records.title: Plant reproduction
records.subject: Biology
records.shortDescription: Inspect anthers, stigma, style and ovary.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Flowering plants reproduce sexually through processes connecting flowers, gametes, seeds and new plants. Plants can also reproduce asexually.
explanation: Inspect anthers, stigma, style and ovary.

The representative angiosperm sequence separates pollen transfer, pollen-tube growth and gamete fusion. In typical double fertilization one sperm joins the egg and another joins the central cell with two polar nuclei. Ovules develop into seeds; ovaries generally contribute to fruits. This sequence does not represent all plant groups or asexual methods.
A flowering garden plant can produce seeds that establish new plants under suitable conditions.

records.title: Living and non-living things

records.shortDescription: A plant has cells and life processes.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Living and nonliving examples are distinguished by considering several biological properties together.
explanation: A plant has cells and life processes.

The primary-level comparison includes a plant, animal, viable seed, rock and flame. Living organisms have cells and organized life processes. A seed can be living while a rolling stone is nonliving.

records.title: Fertilization in flowering plants
records.subject: Biology
records.shortDescription: A tube progresses toward an ovule.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Fertilization in flowering plants follows compatible pollen-tube growth and involves fusion events within an ovule.
explanation: A tube progresses toward an ovule.

In the typical angiosperm example, one sperm fuses with an egg to form a diploid zygote. A second sperm fuses with the central cell containing two polar nuclei, usually producing a triploid primary endosperm nucleus. The zygote develops into the embryo; endosperm supports nutrition. The simplified view does not model every species variation.
A seed develops with an embryo and supporting tissues after successful reproductive development.

The simplified view does not model every species variation.

records.shortDescription: The seed contains a living embryo.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Seed germination is the resumption of embryo growth in a viable seed under suitable conditions.
explanation: The seed contains a living embryo.

Water uptake, metabolic activation and embryo development lead to emergence, commonly with the radicle first. Oxygen and appropriate temperature are needed for many seeds; light and dormancy requirements vary. The selected dicot-like sequence is staged and does not predict germination time, success or every species’ cotyledon position.
Seeds from the same batch can germinate differently if water availability or dormancy state differs.

Mass farther from an axis contributes more rotational inertia.

The 60° prism receives all three representative wavelengths at common 55° incidence. Snell’s law determines internal and exit directions using chosen n=1.5+0.004/λ² with λ in micrometres. The selected model has greater deviation for shorter wavelengths; it is not a measured named glass or a complete continuous spectrum.
White light can spread into wavelength components after a glass prism.

records.title: Resonance
records.subject: Physics
records.shortDescription: The natural frequency is fixed at 1 Hz.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: A periodically driven oscillator can respond strongly near its characteristic frequency, with damping controlling amplitude and phase.
explanation: The natural frequency is fixed at 1 Hz.

The steady-state linear model has natural frequency 1 Hz and static displacement F₀/k=0.1 m. Gain is 1/√[(1−r²)²+(2ζr)²]. For displacement, the nonzero-frequency maximum lies at r=√(1−2ζ²) when ζ<1/√2; stronger damping removes that peak. No initial transient is included.
A driven mechanical system responds differently as drive frequency crosses its natural scale.

definitions.Damping ratio: Dimensionless measure of linear damping relative to critical damping.
definitions.Phase lag: Delay in the response cycle relative to the drive.

records.formula: Gain=[(1−r²)²+(2ζr)²]⁻½; r=ω/ω₀

records.title: Doppler effect

records.shortDescription: Choose emitted frequency.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Relative motion between a sound source and observer changes the received frequency.

records.subject: Physics
records.shortDescription: Use 300 K and 2 L at the selected fixed gas amount.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Thermodynamics relates heat, work and changes in state. For a chosen monatomic ideal gas, internal energy depends on temperature.
explanation: Use 300 K and 2 L at the selected fixed gas amount.

The chamber shows equilibrium ideal-gas states with U=3nRT/2. Added readouts compare the selected state with 300 K and 2 L. The explicit reversible comparison path first changes temperature at fixed 2 L, then changes volume isothermally at the final temperature. Work by the gas is nRT ln(V/2 L), and Q=ΔU+W. The displayed particles do not compute collisions or a real process trajectory.
A gas can receive heat while doing work during a controlled expansion.

records.title: Entropy
records.subject: Physics
records.shortDescription: Use T₀=300 K and V₀=2 L.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Entropy is a state quantity. Changes can be calculated along a reversible comparison path even when an actual process is irreversible.
explanation: Use T₀=300 K and V₀=2 L.

For the selected monatomic ideal gas relative to 300 K and 2 L, ΔS=n(3R/2)ln(T/300)+nRln(V/2). This is the gas entropy change, not the total entropy of gas plus surroundings. A gas entropy decrease is possible when surroundings compensate; the second law concerns the total isolated system. The chamber prescribes equilibrium states rather than simulating irreversibility.
An ideal-gas isothermal expansion increases the gas entropy as accessible volume increases.
scientificPrinciples: For the selected monatomic ideal gas relative to 300 K and 2 L, ΔS=n(3R/2)ln(T/300)+nRln(V/2). This is the gas entropy change, not the total entropy of gas plus surroundings. realLifeExamples: An ideal-gas isothermal expansion increases the gas entropy as accessible volume increases.

records.title: Centre of mass
records.subject: Physics
records.shortDescription: Set mass 1 while mass 2 remains 1 kg.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: The centre of mass is the mass-weighted mean position of a system.
explanation: Set mass 1 while mass 2 remains 1 kg.

Two point masses on a massless rod rotate about their centre of mass. Mass 2 is fixed at 1 kg; mass 1 and separation are adjustable. Distances satisfy m₁r₁=m₂r₂, with masses on opposite sides. The model prescribes rotation and does not solve external forces or a full body’s distributed mass.
A balanced two-mass system has its centre closer to the heavier mass.

records.title: Viscosity
records.subject: Physics
records.shortDescription: Use a Newtonian incompressible liquid.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Viscosity characterizes internal resistance to relative fluid motion. In a Newtonian fluid, shear stress is proportional to shear rate.
explanation: Use a Newtonian incompressible liquid.

The fully developed laminar pipe example uses dynamic viscosity η in Poiseuille’s relation. At fixed radius, pressure drop and length, volume flow varies inversely with η. The parabolic profile is zero at the no-slip wall and maximum at the centre. This model excludes non-Newtonian behaviour and turbulence.
A more viscous Newtonian liquid flows more slowly through the same ideal tube under the same pressure drop.
scientificPrinciples: The fully developed laminar pipe example uses dynamic viscosity η in Poiseuille’s relation. At fixed radius, pressure drop and length, volume flow varies inversely with η. The parabolic profile is zero at the no-slip wall and maximum at the centre. This model excludes non-Newtonian behaviour and turbulence.

definitions.Dynamic viscosity: Proportionality between shear stress and shear rate in a Newtonian fluid, in Pa·s.
definitions.No-slip condition: Fluid velocity matches a stationary solid wall at the boundary.

records.formula: Q=πr⁴Δp/(8ηL); vmax=2vmean
realLifeExamples: A more viscous Newtonian liquid flows more slowly through the same ideal tube under the same pressure drop.

records.title: Immune system

records.shortDescription: Observe the barrier example.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: The immune system combines barriers, innate responses and adaptive responses to recognize and respond to biological challenges.
explanation: Observe the barrier example.

Barrier surfaces can limit entry; innate cells recognize and respond to common signals; adaptive B and T cells support specific responses and memory. The examples stage engulfment, antibody representation and memory without calculating infection or protection probabilities. Immune regulation and tolerance are also important beyond these scenes.
Skin and mucous membranes contribute defence before deeper immune responses are needed.

records.title: Diffusion and osmosis
records.subject: Biology
records.shortDescription: Solute exchange occurs at fixed water volumes.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Diffusion is net spreading associated with random molecular motion. Osmosis specifically concerns solvent movement across a selectively permeable barrier.
explanation: Diffusion is net spreading associated with random molecular motion. Osmosis specifically concerns solvent movement across a selectively permeable barrier.

Diffusion mode exchanges solute at fixed equal volumes with exact concentration relaxation. Osmosis mode keeps solutes impermeant and moves water down its chemical-potential tendency using ideal dilute osmotic pressure at 298.15 K and no opposing hydrostatic pressure. Total water remains 2 L; each side retains its initial solute in osmosis mode.
A selectively permeable plant-cell membrane can support osmotic water movement, while a dissolved dye can diffuse in water.
scientificPrinciples: Diffusion mode exchanges solute at fixed equal volumes with exact concentration relaxation. Osmosis mode keeps solutes impermeant and moves water down its chemical-potential tendency using ideal dilute osmotic pressure at 298.15 K and no opposing hydrostatic pressure. Total water remains 2 L; each side retains its initial solute in osmosis mode.

definitions.Diffusion: Net transport associated with random motion and concentration differences under the stated conditions.
definitions.Osmosis: Net solvent movement across a selectively permeable barrier under a chemical-potential difference.

explanation: Z counts protons.

records.title: Periodic trends
records.subject: Chemistry
records.shortDescription: Distinguish radius from ionization energy.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Periodic trends summarize recurring tendencies in properties, with important exceptions and dependence on the property definition.
explanation: Distinguish radius from ionization energy.

Across many main-group periods, atomic size tends to decrease and first ionization energy tends to increase as effective nuclear attraction changes. Down many groups, additional shells tend to increase size. Subshell structure, shielding, electron pairing and different radius definitions produce exceptions. The viewer marks qualitative directions without fabricating measured values.
Comparing alkali metals down a group requires considering additional electron shells.
scientificPrinciples: Across many main-group periods, atomic size tends to decrease and first ionization energy tends to increase as effective nuclear attraction changes. Down many groups, additional shells tend to increase size. Subshell structure, shielding, electron pairing and different radius definitions produce exceptions. The viewer marks qualitative directions without fabricating measured values.

definitions.First ionization energy: Energy required to remove an electron from a gas-phase neutral atom in its ground state.
definitions.Shielding: Reduction of nuclear attraction experienced by an electron due to other electrons.

records.formula: Qualitative main-group tendency: across a period radius ↓ and first ionization energy ↑
realLifeExamples: Comparing alkali metals down a group requires considering additional electron shells.
objectives: Distinguish radius from ionization energy.
Nuclear charge and shielding influence electrons.
Subshells and pairing alter simple patterns.
prerequisites: Read element symbols, bond conventions and the stated model assumptions
misconceptions: A trend is not an exception-free numerical law, and all definitions of atomic radius are not identical.

records.title: Metallic bonding
records.subject: Chemistry
records.shortDescription: The lattice represents positive ion cores.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Metallic bonding involves positive ion-core organization and delocalized electronic states extending through the material.
explanation: The lattice represents positive ion cores.

A simple classical Drude model connects carrier density n, charge e, relaxation time τ and electron mass m with σ=ne²τ/m. The chosen carrier density is 8.5×10²⁸ m⁻³, not a universal value for all metals. Electron drift opposes the electric field, while conventional current follows it. Band structure and microscopic collisions are omitted.
Many metals conduct because mobile electronic carriers respond to an applied field.

Band structure and microscopic collisions are omitted.

records.title: Hydrogen bonding
records.subject: Chemistry
records.shortDescription: Find oxygen and two hydrogens.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Hydrogen bonding is a directional interaction involving an appropriate hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor.
explanation: Find oxygen and two hydrogens.

The selected water pair distinguishes covalent O–H bonds within molecules from an intermolecular O–H···O guide. The geometry uses a 104.5° water angle and controlled O–O separation. Its guide does not compute binding energy, lifetime or the probability of a hydrogen bond. Hydrogen bonding can also occur within suitable larger molecules.
Hydrogen bonding contributes to water’s collective properties and many biological structures.
scientificPrinciples: The selected water pair distinguishes covalent O–H bonds within molecules from an intermolecular O–H···O guide. The geometry uses a 104.5° water angle and controlled O–O separation. Its guide does not compute binding energy, lifetime or the probability of a hydrogen bond. Hydrogen bonding can also occur within suitable larger molecules.

records.title: Polymers
records.subject: Chemistry
records.shortDescription: Ethene can contribute to an addition polymer.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Polymers contain many repeat-derived structural units connected into large molecules.
explanation: Ethene can contribute to an addition polymer.

The ethene-derived chain fragment displays [–CH₂–CH₂–]ₙ. End groups and molecular-weight distributions are omitted, so it is not a complete finite-molecule formula. Actual polymers differ in branching, stereochemistry, composition and structure. The small prescribed chain motion is an inspection aid, not a polymerization-rate or force-field simulation.
Changing chain structure can affect material properties, but those properties need a model beyond a short fragment.

detailedExplanation: Ethene can contribute to an addition polymer.

The ethene-derived chain fragment displays [–CH₂–CH₂–]ₙ. End groups and molecular-weight distributions are omitted, so it is not a complete finite-molecule formula. Actual polymers differ in branching, stereochemistry, composition and structure. The small prescribed chain motion is an inspection aid, not a polymerization-rate or force-field simulation.
Changing chain structure can affect material properties, but those properties need a model beyond a short fragment.
A repeat-unit formula is not automatically the exact formula of a finite terminated chain.

records.title: Intermolecular forces
records.subject: Chemistry
records.shortDescription: Internal bonds and between-particle forces differ.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Intermolecular interactions act between particles and differ from the covalent connectivity within molecules.
explanation: Internal bonds and between-particle forces differ.

The viewer compares a chosen Lennard-Jones pair potential with polar-water and hydrogen-bond geometries. Dispersion occurs for all polarizable particles; permanent dipoles and suitable donor/acceptor patterns add other contributions. The Lennard-Jones parameters are teaching choices and do not quantify every interaction in water.
Both polar and nonpolar substances can experience dispersion interactions.

records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Biomolecules include diverse chemical structures supporting energy use, cellular organization, information and regulation.
explanation: Glucose illustrates carbohydrate connectivity.

Open-chain glucose connectivity and neutral glycine connectivity provide two small examples. Glucose commonly has cyclic forms in aqueous conditions, while glycine’s ionic state depends on pH and other conditions. The gallery does not depict complete protein folding, DNA, lipid assemblies or biomolecular stereochemistry.
Amino acids can contribute residues to proteins, while sugars participate in energy and structural chemistry.

records.title: Plate tectonics
records.subject: Earth & Space
records.shortDescription: Plate tectonics describes motion and interaction of lithospheric plates, with distinct boundary behaviours.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Plate tectonics describes motion and interaction of lithospheric plates, with distinct boundary behaviours.
explanation: Plate tectonics describes motion and interaction of lithospheric plates, with distinct boundary behaviours.

The staged view compares divergent, convergent and transform boundaries. A chosen relative speed in cm/year gives displacement over a compressed one-million-year interval. Oceanic spreading and subduction participate in redistribution of lithosphere.

records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Oceans exchange heat, water and materials with the atmosphere and continents and support diverse ecosystems.
explanation: Oceans exchange heat, water and materials with the atmosphere and continents and support diverse ecosystems.

The selected cross-section isolates how surface-water temperature and salinity influence a linear density approximation. Denser water is assigned a sinking tendency and lighter water a rising tendency. Real circulation also depends on wind, Earth’s rotation, pressure, mixing and basin geometry; a two-column diagram is not the global ocean conveyor.
Cooling or increasing salinity can increase density in the model’s surface-water range.

records.ageAppropriateExplanation: The Sun is a star whose radiation supplies much of the energy driving Earth’s surface systems.

The photospheric blackbody example uses nominal effective temperature 5772 K and a solar radius. Luminosity follows 4πR²σT⁴ and peak wavelength follows Wien’s relationship. Sunlight supports photosynthesis and influences Earth’s energy balance.

records.shortDescription: The Solar System contains the Sun, eight planets and many other objects with diverse physical properties and orbits.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: The Solar System contains the Sun, eight planets and many other objects with diverse physical properties and orbits.
explanation: The Solar System contains the Sun, eight planets and many other objects with diverse physical properties and orbits.

The original observatory shows the eight planets with approximate orbital periods and compressed sizes and distances. Rocky terrestrial planets differ from giant planets, and dwarf planets, moons and small bodies extend the system beyond those eight. The circular coplanar model is not a precise ephemeris or scale model.
Earth and Jupiter both orbit the Sun but differ greatly in size, composition and orbital period.

Increasing black-hole mass increases the Schwarzschild radius proportionally.

records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Quantum states are described by wavefunctions whose probability predictions differ from classical particle paths.
explanation: Quantum states are described by wavefunctions whose probability predictions differ from classical particle paths.

One electron in a one-dimensional infinite well has quantized energies n²h²/(8mL²). records.title: Relativity
records.subject: Physics
records.shortDescription: Special relativity relates measurements between inertial observers while preserving the same vacuum light speed.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Special relativity relates measurements between inertial observers while preserving the same vacuum light speed.
explanation: Special relativity relates measurements between inertial observers while preserving the same vacuum light speed.

The transverse light-clock example uses γ=1/√(1−β²) and proper time τ=t/γ. A moving clock’s light follows a longer diagonal path in lab coordinates, while its speed remains c. The finite display restarts an inertial segment; acceleration, gravitational effects and a twin-paradox turnaround are excluded.
Different inertial descriptions can assign different elapsed coordinate times without a mechanical fault in a clock.
